questions.stem: Which screening approach is recommended by the USPSTF for an otherwise eligible woman age 65 years or older without known osteoporosis or a prior fragility fracture?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Screen with DXA bone mineral density, with or without fracture-risk assessment.","B":"Use a serum calcium level alone as the osteoporosis screening test.","C":"Use a routine hip radiograph instead of bone-density testing.","D":"Do not screen unless a fracture has already occurred."}}
questions.rationale: The USPSTF 2025 recommendation advises screening women 65 years or older for osteoporosis. Screening includes DXA bone mineral density, with or without fracture-risk assessment. Serum calcium and routine radiography are not substitutes for osteoporosis screening.
questions.source_name: USPSTF — Osteoporosis to Prevent Fractures: Screening
questions.source_detail: Final recommendation January 14, 2025; implementation: screen women age 65 years or older with DXA BMD, with or without fracture-risk assessment.

questions.stem: Why is glaucoma screening with a comprehensive dilated eye examination particularly important for people at increased risk?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Glaucoma commonly causes obvious pain before any optic-nerve damage occurs.","B":"Glaucoma often has no early symptoms, and vision loss may be irreversible once it occurs.","C":"Glaucoma is diagnosed reliably by a routine blood test before eye changes develop.","D":"Glaucoma affects only people who already have severe central vision loss."}}
questions.rationale: The National Eye Institute states that glaucoma often has no symptoms at first. A comprehensive dilated eye examination is used to detect glaucoma, and early treatment can help prevent further irreversible vision loss.
questions.source_detail: Updated 2025-2026 content: early symptoms often none; diagnosis includes comprehensive dilated eye examination; early treatment can protect vision.

questions.stem: An older adult has declining vision and slowed reaction time and asks whether age alone means driving must stop immediately. Which nursing approach is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Assess driving-related functional abilities and discuss referral for a formal driving evaluation when concerns are identified.","B":"Recommend that every older adult stop driving solely because of chronological age.","C":"Ignore vision and reaction-time changes because clinicians have no role in driving-safety counseling.","D":"Assume that one abnormal office measure automatically proves the person is unsafe to drive."}}
questions.rationale: NHTSA guidance for clinicians supports individualized assessment of driving-related vision, cognition, and motor/sensory function and counseling or referral when concerns are identified. Chronological age alone is not an adequate determination of driving fitness.
questions.source_name: NHTSA — Clinician's Guide to Assessing and Counseling Older Drivers
questions.source_detail: NHTSA older-driver guidance: clinical assessment of driving-related skills evaluates vision, cognition, and motor/sensory function and supports individualized counseling and referral.

questions.stem: A client spends several hours each day performing repetitive handwashing rituals in response to intrusive contamination fears and experiences marked distress when unable to complete them. Which condition is most consistent with this pattern?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Obsessive-compulsive disorder","B":"A normal preference for cleanliness","C":"Antisocial personality disorder","D":"A contagious skin infection"}}
questions.rationale: OCD involves recurring intrusive thoughts or urges and repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response. NIMH specifically lists excessive cleaning or handwashing as a common compulsion and notes that clinically significant symptoms are time-consuming, distressing, or impairing.
questions.source_name: NIMH — Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: When Unwanted Thoughts or Repetitive Behaviors Take Over
questions.source_detail: Signs and symptoms: obsessions and compulsions; excessive cleaning or handwashing; symptoms commonly consume more than 1 hour daily or cause significant distress/interference.

questions.stem: A client is preoccupied with a slight or unnoticeable perceived flaw in appearance, repeatedly checks mirrors and seeks reassurance, and has substantial social impairment. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Body dysmorphic disorder","B":"A normal level of appearance concern","C":"Delirium","D":"A primary infectious skin disorder"}}
questions.rationale: The American Psychiatric Association describes body dysmorphic disorder as preoccupation with perceived appearance flaws that are not noticeable or appear slight to others, accompanied by repetitive behaviors such as mirror checking or reassurance seeking and clinically significant distress or impairment.
questions.source_name: American Psychiatric Association — Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders
questions.source_detail: Body Dysmorphic Disorder section: perceived flaws not noticeable or slight to others; repetitive mirror checking/reassurance seeking; significant distress or functional impairment.

questions.stem: A client has persistent fear of being scrutinized or negatively judged in social situations, avoids eating or speaking in front of others, and the fear interferes with daily functioning. Which condition best fits this pattern?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Social anxiety disorder","B":"Normal introversion without impairment","C":"Antisocial personality disorder","D":"Delirium"}}
questions.rationale: NIMH describes social anxiety disorder as fear or anxiety in situations where a person may be scrutinized, evaluated, or judged by others, often producing avoidance and functional impairment. Eating in front of others and public speaking are specifically cited examples.
questions.source_name: NIMH — Social Anxiety Disorder: What You Need to Know
questions.source_detail: Definition and signs/symptoms: fear of scrutiny, evaluation, judgment, embarrassment or rejection; avoidance; interference with daily life.

questions.stem: A client with influenza asks about the importance of antiviral timing. Which teaching is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Clinical benefit is greatest when treatment starts as soon as possible, ideally within 48 hours, but later treatment may still benefit hospitalized, severe, progressive, or high-risk patients.","B":"Antivirals have no benefit if more than exactly 48 hours have passed.","C":"Treatment should be delayed until symptoms have nearly resolved.","D":"Timing has no relationship to antiviral benefit."}}
questions.rationale: CDC 2026 guidance states that influenza antiviral treatment provides the greatest benefit when started early, especially within 48 hours. However, treatment can still provide benefit after 48 hours in hospitalized patients, patients with severe or progressive illness, and people at increased risk for complications.
questions.source_name: CDC — Influenza Antiviral Medications: Summary for Clinicians
questions.source_detail: Updated March 10, 2026: benefit greatest when started early, especially within 48 hours; later treatment can still benefit hospitalized/severe/progressive/high-risk patients.

questions.stem: A client with prior liver disease is receiving systemic fluconazole and develops rising aminotransferases. What should the nurse recognize?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Fluconazole can cause serious hepatic toxicity, so abnormal liver tests require monitoring for worsening hepatic injury.","B":"Fluconazole has no clinically important hepatic adverse effects.","C":"Abnormal liver tests should be ignored unless blood glucose is also elevated.","D":"Fluconazole-associated liver injury occurs only after a predictable cumulative dose."}}
questions.rationale: Fluconazole labeling warns of rare serious hepatic toxicity and advises caution in patients with liver dysfunction. Patients who develop abnormal liver function tests during therapy should be monitored for more severe hepatic injury, and the drug should be discontinued if clinical signs or symptoms of liver disease attributable to fluconazole develop.
questions.source_detail: Warnings, Hepatic Injury: caution with liver dysfunction; monitor patients with abnormal liver function tests for more severe hepatic injury.

questions.stem: A client is receiving intravenous ferumoxytol for iron-deficiency anemia. Which safety measure is required by the current product label?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Observe for hypersensitivity during the infusion and for at least 30 minutes afterward, with treatment for anaphylaxis immediately available.","B":"No observation is needed if a previous dose was tolerated.","C":"Administer the entire dose as a rapid IV push to reduce reaction risk.","D":"Monitor only for hypoglycemia because hypersensitivity is not a labeled concern."}}
questions.rationale: Feraheme (ferumoxytol) carries a boxed warning for serious hypersensitivity and anaphylaxis. The May 31, 2026 label requires administration as an IV infusion over at least 15 minutes with personnel and therapies available to treat anaphylaxis, and observation during and for at least 30 minutes after the infusion.
questions.source_detail: Updated May 31, 2026; Boxed Warning and section 5.1 Serious Hypersensitivity Reactions: infusion over at least 15 minutes; observe during and at least 30 minutes afterward.

questions.stem: A client with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation is switched from warfarin to apixaban and asks whether INR testing will be used routinely to adjust the apixaban dose. Which response is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"No. Apixaban dosing is not routinely titrated to an INR as warfarin is; dose selection follows the labeled indication and patient-specific criteria.","B":"Yes. Apixaban requires the same INR target and routine dose titration as warfarin.","C":"Yes. Apixaban must be held whenever the INR is below 2.0.","D":"No. Laboratory and clinical monitoring are unnecessary for apixaban therapy."}}
questions.rationale: Apixaban has fixed labeled dosing schemes based on indication and specified patient factors rather than routine INR-guided titration. Clinical follow-up, renal/hepatic assessment when appropriate, adherence review, and bleeding surveillance remain important; the absence of routine INR dose adjustment does not mean monitoring is unnecessary.
questions.source_detail: Dosage and Administration section 2.1: indication-specific fixed dosing and NVAF dose-reduction criteria; INR-based titration is not part of labeled apixaban dosing.
